en: The proof of the non-authoritativeness of the Vedas:
that which has no necessary connection with something does not possess authoritativeness with respect to it,
just as a donkey, which is unconnected to fire, lacks authoritativeness regarding it.

And Vedic words are unconnected with external objects; this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). That Vedic words refer to external objects—this reason (*hetu*) is not, first of all, unestablished (*asiddha*).
Since there is, in reality, no necessary connection between words and their objects,
a necessary connection consists in having a connected nature;
nor can that [connected nature] be without a basis, because it would otherwise follow that everything would have a connected nature with respect to everything.
Furthermore, no basis for this [cognition] other than identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) is possible;
for that which does not have the nature of something else, nor arises from it, lacks a nature that is necessarily connected to it.
Moreover, words do not possess the nature of external objects, because they are the objects of cognitions that appear as distinct.
Nor do words arise from external objects,
because it is observed that words are produced even in the absence of an object, since their occurrence is dependent upon the intention of a person.
It is not perceived;
for indeed, by virtue of its very fitness, something is perceived as having a nature that is restricted to a particular place.
Just as the visual faculty,
when the eye is indeed being exercised upon a form, perceives only that form,
so too these Vedic words, although devoid of identity with or production from their objects, will cause the supersensuous meaning to be understood by means of mere capacity alone.

How then, in the mere absence of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), could there be no causal necessity (*apratibandha*), by which this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) would be established?
Thus it is indeed these [two].
R: *bodha*; MS: *tādātmya*; R: *yenaivaṃ*
"It is established"—
this is not a fault,
because even the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) is restricted to illuminating only visible form (*rūpa*), excluding taste and so forth, since it has that as its specific effect (*tatkāryatva*).
For form assists the eye;
indeed, the eye does not illuminate form by its mere existence,
because otherwise it would follow that even a form obstructed [by a barrier] could be perceived.
Therefore, it is clearly determined that the eye produces the cognition of form by attaining the capacity to generate that cognition when the form is present in a suitable location;
otherwise, for one who does not depend on such assistance, the restriction that it illuminates only that [form] would be untenable.
For, if there were no distinction in being unassisted, the restriction that the eye is the illuminator of form alone and not of taste and so forth would not be possible.
In that case, from where does this restriction derive— that the eye must be assisted by visible form alone, and not by taste and so forth?
This [restriction] is not [established].
Even when there is no distinction in the nature of the cognition of form,
a restriction [regarding the object] is established.

If form assists [the sense] solely by the power of the thing-in-itself (*vastuvaśāt*) and not taste and so forth— well then, just as the restriction of the eye’s capacity to be assisted by form is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*), let there likewise be an intrinsic restriction for words in the communication of external objects.
°kāryatvaṃ prati° is missing in R; R has *ca* before *cakṣu°*; MS contains a mistaken doubling of *ca*.
To this it is replied:
there is no inherent restriction of the eye to being assisted by form,
because it is impossible for any entity to possess an inherent nature [in that regard].
For thus, those who concede that an intrinsic nature (svābhāvikatva) is a property of things must be questioned:
"What is this 'intrinsic'? Does it arise from itself, or does it arise from another?
Or is it indeed causeless?
If it arises from itself, that is inconsistent because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself;
if, on the other hand, it is causeless, that is untenable.
Since it is impossible for there to be a restriction of place and so forth in the absence of a cause,
the specific determination of the eye’s capacity to assist form cannot be inherent;
what, then, is its basis?
We say that it is dependent on its own cause:
indeed, the eye, being produced by its own cause, is produced as precisely such that it can only be assisted by visible form;
and visible form also is produced by its own cause as precisely such that it has the nature of assisting that [eye].
The necessity of being an effect;
[it] should be asked of one who follows [the consequence].
R is missing;
then, not from a cause; R is missing; R is missing.

If it is argued that even for words, that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is likewise dependent solely upon their own causes, by virtue of which they do not deviate from external objects— this is not found in manuscript R.
It is not possible to state [a solution] because the Vedic sentences are accepted as being eternal;
yet, if this objection is intended to be refuted by accepting their non-eternality, that too is difficult to maintain due to the consequence of further faults.

For if they were produced by their own causes as possessing the power to indicate a fixed meaning, then they would cause even one who has not learned the linguistic convention to understand their own meaning.

Just as the eye, having arisen from its own causes as that which illuminates form, indeed illuminates form even for one who does not know the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), and there is no comprehension of a specific object even before a word has been uttered for one who has not grasped the convention; therefore, it is certain that for words, unlike the eye and other [senses], there is no fixed rule for conveying meaning that is dependent solely upon their own causes.
It is indeed possible that [the text] is for the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha). R reads "niyamārtho," while MS reads "niyathārtho."
svahotaḥ is missing from MS;
saṃmayasyāpi is also [missing] from MS.
The meaning is missing;
cf.
Or rather, it is by their own causes alone that such a capacity has been bestowed upon them, whereby they, assisted only by specific conventions, cause some particular object to be understood;
this is the nature [of things] bestowed.
If the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) were given [by the word], then upon a change of convention, it would not come to denote other objects;
for if this word *agnihotra* denotes a particular sacrifice while depending on a convention, how could it denote a different object through a different convention?

For indeed, a seed that has arisen from its own cause with the nature of producing a sprout— though dependent on soil and other factors— is not capable of producing a donkey; likewise, a word also, being restricted to the communication of a specific object, would manifest only that object when the conventional agreement (*saṃketa*) is reversed.
Or, it might be argued that this [word] has now arisen as something capable of conveying those respective meanings, depending upon those respective conventions (*saṅketa*).
That too is not useful for the present context;
for its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is not established in this way.
Since it is indeed possible that, through convention (*saṅketa*), it might convey a meaning other than what is intended, one cannot determine whether it illuminates only the intended object or not.

If it is argued that, by means of convention (*saṅketa*), there will then be a relationship between the object and the word characterized as the signified and the signifier; R [states]: "By means of convention, not for one who lacks [it]. R [continues]: "In that case, the relationship between the object and the word will be characterized as the signified and the signifier."
And so it has been said:
although the relationships between the signified and the signifier exist as real entities,
[they remain] unidentified.
If it is argued that "those [particulars], not being manifested by conventions, are not the causes for the manifestation of meaning," we reply:
surely, if they were real, it would follow— as has already been stated— that even one who does not know the convention would have a cognition of the meaning.

And since it was previously stated that words do not apply to other objects when there is dependence on convention, this relationship characterized as the signifier-signified (vācya-vācaka) has already been refuted; therefore,
the conclusion is that words have no necessary connection with external objects.
That which is the cognition of the meaning. MS arthapratīta MS cf.
25.2–4 Or [it] does not proceed, etc. (MS *pravartanti*; R *pravartetetyādi*).
They proceed (MS); "they would proceed," etc. (R);
not prescribed (MS); cf.
Consequently, the reason is neither unestablished nor contradictory, because there is no pervasion by the opposite.
And its absence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) is demonstrated by showing its occurrence there;
for it is not logical that a contradictory [reason] should exist in a subject possessing the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*),
because the opposite of the property to be proven is absent therein.
Furthermore, there is no possibility of the pervaded existing without the pervader, for that would entail its loss of identity;
nor is this reason inconclusive, because there exists a subverting proof [bādhaka] against the contrary.
When the negation of validity is the probandum, validity itself is the counter-example (vipakṣa);
and in that case, there is no reason characterized by the absence of a necessary connection (pratibandha),
because [the reason] is pervaded by a connection that is contrary to itself.

Indeed, this term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is not merely local; it cannot be without a basis in the case of cognitions, for otherwise it would follow that the designation "means of valid cognition" would apply to all cognitions indiscriminately.
Furthermore, no basis other than the connection with its own object is logically possible.

Therefore, the state of being the object of the designation "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa) for a means of valid cognition is pervaded by the existence of a necessary connection with its own object; consequently, since the exclusion of the counter-example is established through the perception of a property that is pervaded by the opposite [of the probandum], the reason is not inconclusive,
nor is any other fault possible.
Therefore, that which is established by a reason from which all defects have been eliminated must indeed be accepted by the wise;
[this is so] because of the impossibility of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the case of a probans based on similarity (*sādharmya*).
Because of arising there,
[and] because of death and rebirth; MS lacks "R".
Because there exists a subverting means of valid cognition (bādhakapramāṇa) regarding the probandum (sādhya).
By means of the non-perception [of validity] in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa)—

that is, by perceiving in the subject (dharmin) that is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) the absence of validity, which is pervaded by its opposite— one excludes [validity] from the dissimilar instance.
The Proof of the Non-authoritativeness of the Vedas, a work by Paṇḍita Jitāri.
